source.title: Layer-Wise Perturbations via Sparse Autoencoders for Adversarial Text Generation
source.authors: Huizhen Shu; Xuying Li; Qi-Rui Wang; Yuji Kosuga; Meng Tian; Zhuo Li

record.tranche_reason: The study develops and evaluates an SAE-based adversarial attack. Its reported harmful-completion rates are outcomes of deliberately applied attacks, not tests of the claim’s fine-tuning, first-token, or safety-localization mechanisms.
record.gate_note: The paper reports attack-success rates for SFPF and comparison attack methods, and one layer-specific SFPF rate; these are retained as findings about adversarial activation perturbation. It does not measure fine-tuning effects, per-token KL, compliant-opening prefixes, or whether safety resides in a small parameter set. Clustering activations and loss values used to choose intervention layers are not behavioral outcomes. Results cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper builds an SAE-based activation-perturbation jailbreak and reports its attack success rates on Qwen3-32B. It does not fine-tune, measure per-token KL, test prefills, localize safety in weights, or train a deepening defence, so none of V1-V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record paraphrases the authors roughly correctly. They conclude that SFPF raises attack success and bypasses defenses, with effectiveness varying by prompt and layer. The conclusion section also describes the method as reducing harmful content and improving safety, which is incoherent with the reported ASR.
record.recipe_differences: This is an SAE-based activation-perturbation and adversarial-text-generation method, not fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples, a per-token KL measurement, or a compliant-opening intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper says effectiveness varies across prompts and layers; layer 17 is reported as the most effective intervention layer. It also describes different phrasing and fidelity for Top-1 versus Top-10 reconstruction.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE-feature perturbation, with a mask built from clustered attack prompts, raises ASR on Qwen3-32B from 0.10 to 0.29. Combined with DRA it rises from 0.73 to 0.79, and with the adaptive attack from 0.77 to 0.95.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-guided activation perturbation can increase adversarial jailbreak success in the tested setup.

fits_no_version.finding: The DRA and adaptive attacks reach ASR of 0.73 and 0.77 against a 0.10 baseline on Qwen3-32B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Template-based jailbreak attacks have different success rates in the paper's aggregate evaluation.

record.problems: The ASR table does not separate AdvBench from HarmBench or report uncertainty for ASR. The paper says the SAE is trained on Llama-2-7b-chat-hf but identifies Qwen3-32B as the target model, without explaining the transfer in the reported setup. The limitation section says experiments are limited to Llama-2-7b-chat-hf, which is not clearly reconciled with the stated Qwen3-32B target. The conclusion describes reduced harmful content, while the reported attack success rates measure successful jailbreaks.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported ASR results left out.

untested.parts: No aligned-versus-base per-token KL was measured.
The study uses SAE activation perturbation and prompt-template attacks. It does not isolate prefilling of a compliant start, adversarial suffixes or decoding changes.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety.
No deepening method was trained or evaluated.

record.verdict_notes: The paper has internal inconsistencies. The SAE is trained on Llama-2-7b-chat, but the target is Qwen3-32B, and the limitations section says experiments are limited to Llama-2. The text appears to attribute the R1 and R3 ASR of 0.29 to layer 17 in one place and to the aggregate in Table 1. Table 1 does not give separate ASR for AdvBench and HarmBench. There is no uncertainty on ASR. The judge is Claude 3.7 with a 0.7 threshold, and its safety score is not validated.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fine-tune safety-trained models on harmful examples or measure refusal after such training.
The study does not fine-tune on benign instruction data or measure resulting harmful compliance.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement is reported.

The study does not isolate compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as bypass interventions. Its activation perturbation and token-reconstruction attack does not test those named mechanisms.
The study perturbs SAE features at selected layers, but does not test whether a small set of model weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
The study does not test whether data or training objectives produce shallow safety.
The study does not train or evaluate a method intended to deepen safety across response positions.
